title: Investigating Suspicious Authentication Activity
summary: A triage runbook for anomalous logins, impossible travel and privilege changes.
content:
# Investigating Suspicious Authentication Activity

## Scope
Use this runbook for authentication events that are individually plausible but anomalous in
context: a login from a new country, a session at an unusual hour, a privilege escalation
outside a change window, a service account authenticating interactively.

## Signals worth investigating
Impossible travel - two successful authentications from locations too far apart for the
elapsed time. Logins outside the established hours of the user or from an unfamiliar device.
Authentication from a hosting provider or anonymising network for an account that normally
connects from corporate ranges. A service account used interactively when it should only ever
authenticate non-interactively. MFA fatigue: repeated push notifications until one is
approved. A dormant account waking up.

Privilege changes deserve their own attention: an account added to an administrative group, a
new local administrator created, a role assignment outside a recorded change ticket.

## Investigation sequence
Establish a baseline for the account first - normal hours, usual source ranges, typical
devices, which systems it usually touches. An anomaly only means something against a
baseline.

Then build the timeline. Pull every authentication event for the account across the window,
successful and failed. Note the first anomalous event and work outward: what happened
immediately before it, and what did the account do afterwards? Look specifically for actions
that extend access - new credentials or keys created, MFA devices enrolled, mailbox rules
added, group memberships changed.

Correlate across sources. An authentication event alone rarely settles a question; pair it
with VPN logs, endpoint telemetry and network flows for the same window.

## Resolution
Confirm with the user out of band, through a channel other than the one under suspicion. If
the activity is unauthorised, disable the account, invalidate its sessions and tokens, rotate
its credentials and any keys it holds, and review every action it took during the exposure
window. Escalate to a full incident if the account had administrative rights or accessed
sensitive data.

If the activity turns out to be legitimate, record why in the anomaly evidence so the same
pattern is triaged faster next time, and consider tuning the rule that raised it.
